The reports, probably about the same aircraft, come ahead of Russian President Vladimir Putin's arrival in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen for this week's summit of APEC leaders. China and Russia have close diplomatic and military ties.
Taiwan's defence ministry said that after flying through airspace to the island's east, the Russian aircraft, whose type it did not identify, exited its air defence identification zone south of the eastern county of Taitung.
The ministry used joint intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance means to monitor the full course of the activity and "responded appropriately", it added in a brief statement, without giving details.
Earlier on Tuesday, Japan lodged a strong protest to Moscow after two aircraft believed to be Russian violated its airspace off the island of Okinoshima in southwestern Fukuoka, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said.
"The violation of Japan's airspace by Russian aircraft is a serious infringement of Japan's sovereignty," Kihara said, adding that the safety threat was completely unacceptable.
"We lodged a strong protest with Russia and urged it to prevent a recurrence."
The Japan Self-Defense Forces scrambled fighter aircraft and took necessary measures in response, such as issuing warnings and notifications, the country's defence ministry said.
The suspected Russian aircraft were subsequently confirmed to have transited the Tsushima Strait, passed between Yonaguni Island and Taiwan, and proceeded into the Pacific Ocean, it added, also without identifying the aircraft type.
Yonaguni is the Japanese island closest to Taiwan, about 100 km (62 miles) off its east.
OFF TAIWAN'S EAST COAST
A map issued by Japan's defence ministry showed a flight path to Taiwan's east, heading in a southerly direction, implying the aircraft were the same Taiwan spotted later.
The last confirmed violation of Japan's airspace by Russian aircraft was off Rebun Island off Hokkaido, in September 2024, the ministry said.
In 2023, Taiwan spotted two Russian warships off its eastern coast and sent its own aircraft and ships to keep watch.
Taiwan has joined the United States and allies in wide-ranging sanctions against Russia following its invasion of Ukraine.
Over the past six years, democratically governed Taiwan, which China views as its own territory, has regularly reported Chinese navy ships and air force aircraft operating around the island, as Beijing seeks to press its claims.
(Reporting by Ben Blanchard and Kaori Kaneko; Editing by Tom Hogue and Clarence Fernandez)

A131.text:
Razzia bei Sözcü TV Türkische Polizei stürmt Sitz von oppositionsnahem Sender
In der Türkei steht die Pressefreiheit seit Langem massiv unter Druck. Nun hat die regierungstreue Justiz ein weiteres Oppositionsmedium ins Visier genommen. Am frühen Dienstagmorgen haben türkische Sicherheitskräfte eine Razzia am Sitz des oppositionsnahen Senders Sözcü TV und der zugehörigen Mediengruppe in Istanbul ausgeführt und nach deren Angaben mehrere Menschen festgenommen.
»Die Polizei durchsucht das Sözcü-Gebäude aufgrund eines Gerichtsbeschlusses«, teilte die Sözcü-Gruppe am Dienstagmorgen im Onlinedienst X mit. Das Gebäude sei abgeriegelt worden. Ein Zwangsverwalter der Regierung sei eingesetzt worden: »Es hat Festnahmen gegeben.«
Auf der Sözcü-Website hieß es, neben den Räumen von Sözcü TV seien auch die Büros für die Online-Aktivitäten der Gruppe von Antiterroreinheiten durchsucht worden. Ein Zwangsverwalter sei für diese beiden Bereiche eingesetzt worden, nicht aber für die Zeitungsaktivitäten von Sözcü. Sözcü ist von der türkischen Medienaufsicht wiederholt ins Visier genommen worden.
Die türkische Opposition reagierte empört. Man ertrage inzwischen nicht einmal mehr die kleinste Kritik oder dass auch nur eine einzige Wahrheit öffentlich werde, sagte Özgür Özel, Parteichef der im Sommer gegründeten Yeni Parti, türkischen Medien zufolge. Für die Opposition sind die Angriffe auf die Pressefreiheit ein Problem. Präsident Recep Tayyip Erdoğan hat die Medien im Land in den vergangenen Jahren zunehmend gleichgeschaltet. Eine unabhängige Berichterstattung ist kaum mehr möglich. Stimmen der Opposition haben entsprechende Schwierigkeiten, an die Öffentlichkeit durchzudringen. »Wir werden nicht schweigen, wir werden keine Angst haben und wir werden uns nicht ergeben«, sagte Özel den Berichten zufolge.
Die Razzia bei Sözcü ist der jüngste Schlag der Regierung von Präsident Erdoğan gegen regierungskritische Medien in der Türkei. Mitte Oktober hatte die Regierung bereits die Kontrolle über den oppositionsnahen Fernsehsender Halk TV übernommen, den meistgesehenen Nachrichtensender des Landes. Zuvor hatten die Behörden den Zugang zur unabhängigen Nachrichtenwebsite T24 gesperrt.
Angriffe auf Oppositionsmedien gehen einher mit Börsenskandal
Im Oktober 2025 hatten die türkischen Behörden die Kontrolle über den Sender Tele1 übernommen, einen weiteren oppositionsnahen TV-Sender. Die jüngsten Angriffe auf Medien in der Türkei gehen einher mit einem historischen Börsenskandal, der das Land seit Mitte September erschüttert. Die Verbindungen reichen bis ins nahe Umfeld des Präsidenten. Sözcü TV hatte zuletzt ausführlich darüber berichtet.
Hayri Kozanoğlu, ein Experte für internationalen Handel und Finanzen von der Altınbaş-Universität in Istanbul, sagte dme SPIEGEL kürzlich, er gehe davon aus, dass die Regierung erhebliche Anstrengungen unternehmen werde, um die öffentliche Aufmerksamkeit abzulenken. Er rechnete zudem damit, dass der Druck auf die Opposition nun noch steigen könnte. (Mehr dazu lesen Sie hier.)

A134.text:
Nahe Insel Okinoshima Japan beklagt Verletzung seines Luftraums durch russische Flugzeuge
Japan hat Russland vorgeworfen, seinen Luftraum verletzt zu haben. Zwei mutmaßlich russische Flugzeuge seien am Dienstagmorgen nahe der Insel Okinoshima im Südwesten des Landes in den japanischen Luftraum eingedrungen, sagte Regierungssprecher Minoru Kihara. Japanische Kampfflugzeuge seien aufgestiegen, um die Flugzeuge zu warnen.
»Die Verletzung unseres nationalen Luftraums durch russische Flugzeuge ist nicht nur eine schwerwiegende Verletzung der Souveränität unseres Landes, sondern auch eine Bedrohung für unsere Sicherheit und völlig inakzeptabel«, betonte Kihara. Japan habe über diplomatische Kanäle »sehr scharfen Protest« bei Russland eingelegt.
Die Spannungen zwischen Tokio und Moskau hatten in den vergangenen Wochen zugenommen, nachdem ein japanischer Journalist in Russland wegen Spionagevorwürfen festgenommen worden war (mehr dazu hier ) und Moskau das Russlandgeschäft von Japan Tobacco unter seine Verwaltung gestellt hatte.
Die letzte bestätigte Luftraumverletzung durch russische Maschinen ereignete sich dem Verteidigungsministerium zufolge im September 2024 vor der Insel Rebun in der Präfektur Hokkaido.
Auch Südkorea schickt Kampfjets los
Es war nicht der einzige Vorfall dieser Art. Südkorea meldete am Dienstag, dass russische Militärflugzeuge nach Armeeangaben in die südkoreanische Luftraumüberwachungszone eingedrungen sind. Es seien vorsorglich Kampfjets losgeschickt worden, erklärte der Generalstab. Die russischen Flugzeuge hätten den südkoreanischen Luftraum nicht verletzt.
Die Luftverteidigungszone eines Landes ist größer als sein Luftraum und bezeichnet die Zone, in der aus Gründen der militärischen Luftverteidigung durchquerende Flugzeuge überwacht werden.
Vorfälle dieser Art kommen auch in Osteuropa regelmäßig vor. Wegen einer Bedrohung im Luftraum hatten zuletzt Lettland und Litauen Alarm geschlagen. Am vergangenen Mittwoch seien die Einwohner in mehreren Regionen beider Länder aufgerufen worden, Schutzräume aufzusuchen, teilten die Behörden mit.
Grund dafür waren unbekannte Drohnen, die über das benachbarte Russland oder Belarus in den Luftraum eingedrungen waren. Daraufhin stiegen Kampfflugzeuge der Nato-Luftraumüberwachung auf. Dem Nationalen Krisenmanagementzentrum Litauens zufolge galt die Warnung auch für die zweitgrößte Stadt des Landes, Kaunas, mit rund 300.000 Einwohnern.

A16.text:
Will Netanyahu lose this time?
The Israeli prime minister has manoeuvred out of tough situations before to retain power. But he may find it hard this time.
I have been covering Benjamin Netanyahu for more than 30 years. I was in Washington when, as a young opposition leader, he worked hand in glove with the Republicans to embarrass Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin and sabotage the Oslo Accords. I have seen him cornered before. I have never seen him cornered like this.
The numbers are merciless. His bloc won 53 seats, eight short of a majority. Sixty-seven members of the new Knesset recommended former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, who now has up to 42 days to form a government. For Netanyahu, they may be the longest 42 days of his political life.
The stakes are political, but above all personal. His corruption trial continues, and he faces a possible prison sentence. His pardon request has been gathering dust on President Isaac Herzog’s desk for months. Eisenkot’s bloc has already tabled bills for a state commission of inquiry into the October 7 attacks and for prime-ministerial term limits.
A state inquiry would strip him of the title he covets the most: “defender of Israel”. For Netanyahu, the chair is not a job. It is a lifeline. His trial, under way since May 2020, is in its final stretch. A sitting prime minister can be removed only after a final conviction.
From his office, he can stall hearings and lean on the justice system. Out of office, he is just another defendant.
To survive, Netanyahu does not need to build a government. He needs time to keep his rivals from building one. To buy it, he is pulling three levers.
The first is his proposal for a “national unity government” of all the parties that support Israel as the nation-state of the Jewish people. Translation: the Arab parties, representing 21 percent of the population, are out. The Jewish supremacists, Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, are in. So are the anti-Zionist Haredi parties. This is unity, Netanyahu-style.
He has gift-wrapped the offer in the old rhetoric of the Iranian nuclear threat, with one catch: He would not give up the premiership or agree to a rotation.
Eisenkot has called the offer “another spin”, yet he has agreed to negotiate with Likud. He knows a refusal would only feed the spin machine: They will talk to Arab supporters of Hamas, but not to Jewish patriots, the Netanyahu camp would claim.
He also knows to beware of a diversion designed to burn through the days the president has allotted him.
The second lever is incitement. At the Knesset’s opening session, Netanyahu branded Ra’am and the Joint List “terror supporters” and “haters of Israel”. A government depending on them, he declared, “must not be formed”. The goal is to strangle an Arab-backed government in its cradle, and to scare the Haredi parties, which are currently part of his bloc, away from joining the “enemy”.
But this time the incitement has a hole in it. Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas says Netanyahu’s confidant Natan Eshel sounded him out on the bill to bar an indicted politician from serving as prime minister. Joint List lawmaker Ahmad Tibi went on live television with WhatsApp messages he said came from Eshel. “Terror supporters”, it seems, are good enough for a quiet chat.
The third lever is escalation. According to media reports, Netanyahu has been pressing US President Donald Trump for another wave of strikes on Iran. A return to full-scale war could help him form an emergency government.
In a media interview, former Prime Minister Ehud Barak laid out the scenario: a blatant provocation that forces Iran to respond, and a war that would disrupt or prevent the establishment of a new government. Lebanon, Gaza or the West Bank could serve just as well. The mantra is well-known: The enemy must see that we are united.
Here, too, there are limits.
[truncated]

A17.text:
Palestine Weekly: Israel’s political reshuffle as the occupation grinds on
As Eisenkot’s bloc moves to form a government and courts the ultra-Orthodox, the Gaza genocide and settler pogroms continue.
Israel’s parliament speaker is due to be replaced on Tuesday, one of several signs that power is being rearranged as opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot’s bloc angles to lead the government.
But for Palestinians, the machinery of occupation, dispossession and deprivation keeps running. Israeli attacks killed at least 37 people in Gaza in the past week, while in the occupied West Bank, settlers attacked whole villages with little to stop them.
Gaza: Two narratives of daily killing under the “ceasefire”
The past week saw numerous Israeli attacks and killings in Gaza, as military claims of targeting fighters were weighed against accounts of people killed in tents, filling water containers and driving to a wedding photo shoot. According to Gaza’s Ministry of Health, as of November 16, Israel has killed 1,650 Palestinians since the October 2025 “ceasefire”.
On November 12, an Israeli bomb hit the Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis. The hospital’s surgery building was struck, killing six people, including surgeon Rizq Abu Shaira, and wounding dozens. The Israeli military said it targeted Hamas’s Khan Younis Brigade commander, Muhammad Abu Ismail, and accused Hamas of running a command centre in the hospital. In the days that followed, the foreign ministers of 18 Arab and Muslim-majority countries condemned the attack as a violation of international humanitarian law.
Beyond the hospital bombing, the Israeli military told Israeli media it had killed 10 Hamas operatives in the past week. Among them was Samir Abu Younis, whom the army named as Hamas’s Rafah Brigade commander, killed in a drone strike in al-Mawasi on November 14, which Hamas confirmed. The strike hit a tent for displaced people, wounding two. Over the weekend, in Jabalia camp, two men were killed in a strike the army said targeted “terrorists”, and a separate strike on a Gaza government security post in al-Mawasi, Rafah, killed two people, according to Wafa.
At the same time, Israeli forces continued to kill Palestinians in circumstances that offered little indication of any military target:
- A tank shell hit an apartment in the al-Qastal towers in Deir el-Balah on November 13, where mourners had gathered. Israeli tanks then fired on people fleeing, killing at least three, including 12-year-old Ahmed Abu Daher, and wounding at least 20, according to local activist Hamza al-Masri and Gaza Now.
- According to Wafa, a man was killed by a drone on November 11 as he filled water containers on his Gaza City roof. The next day, a driver taking a groom to a wedding photo shoot in Deir el-Balah was killed by Israeli fire.
- On November 16, a man was shot dead at displacement tents in Jabalia, while three people, including a child, were separately wounded by gunfire inside a school south of Khan Younis, Wafa reported.
This week, Gaza’s Health Ministry recorded the winter’s first death from hypothermia – a nine-month-old baby – following the devastation of last week’s rains. Israel’s Prime Minister’s Office claimed more than 91,000 tents and 8,200 trucks of winter supplies have been delivered, the Times of Israel reported, and blamed Hamas for the suffering. The United Nations, however, reported this week that aid-truck offloads have fallen about 42 percent after Israel suspended the Egyptian corridor.
The United Kingdom, Australia, Canada and Italy called conditions in Gaza “catastrophic” and urged that 150,000 tents be allowed into the territory.
West Bank: Settler attacks, closures and two pogroms
The most violent olive harvest on record continues in the occupied West Bank, as OCHA counted 410 harvest-related attacks this year as of November 9.
[truncated]

A185.text:
Trump in Asia for historic nuclear talks with China and Russia
US President Donald Trump landed in Asia on Monday for economic talks and a planned trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on nuclear issues and the war in Ukraine. Trump also raised the possibility of meeting North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during his visit.
President Donald Trump was heading to Asia on Monday, turning his focus to economic deals and historic three-way nuclear talks with Russia and China as his administration adjusts to a new political reality in Washington. He said he may meet with Kim Jong Un while in China as the US looks to reengage North Korea on its nuclear program.
Trump also said he plans to talk about Russia’s nearly 5-year-old war in Ukraine during his highly anticipated meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin in China.
“We’ll talk about, my favorite subject, Ukraine. Ukraine’s losing Ukraine,” Trump told reporters at the White House on Monday morning before departing for Asia. “Russia is losing 25,000 soldiers in the month. So we’ll be talking about that.”
Trump suggested he’ll talk with the leaders about the war even after his administration officials on Friday told reporters that he would discuss nuclear disarmament and the Iran war with his Chinese and Russian counterparts but steer clear of Russia’s war with Ukraine.
Read moreXi, Trump and Putin to discuss 'world peace' at Shenzhen summit, China says
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had expressed concern as Trump pushed for the meeting with Putin and Xi about the potential of the three leaders using the moment to redraw global spheres of influence.
Planning for the summit has drawn comparisons to the Yalta Conference, the 1945 gathering at which the leaders of the US, Britain and the Soviet Union agreed to divide Germany and Berlin into four military occupation zones and finalised plans for establishing the United Nations.
“We really don’t want this to turn into ‘Yalta 2, 3, 4’ with a redistribution of influence,” Zelenskyy said last month.
After hours of flying, Air Force One had been scheduled to stop in Anchorage, but instead headed to Fairbanks for an Alaska refueling stop. The change wasn’t announced until after the plane landed in Fairbanks and local media began posting pictures.
During the stop, an older model of Air Force One aircraft with the traditional baby blue paint scheme pulled up alongside the Qatari-gifted model, which Trump had been traveling on. There was no sign of Trump during the stop, or of any movement between the planes.
The newer presidential jet later took off, and the White House blamed the change on extreme weather conditions in Anchorage, saying Air Force One landed in Fairbanks in order to refuel in better climate conditions.
Read moreRussia's war on Ukraine: 'Americans want to have a deal whatever the cost for both Ukraine & Europe'
Still, the alternative refueling location called to mind the July incident in Turkey when Trump secretly stowed away on a catering truck to fly out of the country after a NATO summit.
The White House made it appear then that the president was flying on Air Force One — and word of his secret swap didn't emerge until it was first reported by The Washington Post in August.
Trump’s departure follows the often-omnipresent president having remained largely out of public sight for the past several days, even as a nationwide ground stop snarled air traffic and his Republican administration faced tough questions on its handling of the situation.
Trump said he was kept up to date Friday about the ground stop by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who held a briefing Friday evening to address the American public.
Trump defended his decision to delegate to the Cabinet officials to inform the public.
[truncated]

A205.text:
A third American aircraft carrier has arrived in the Middle East, U.S. Central Command said in a social media post Monday, making a dramatic show of military might as U.S. President Donald Trump keeps his options open for next steps in the Iran war.
The USS Theodore Roosevelt brings thousands of additional troops to the Middle East as Trump has oscillated between threatening additional large-scale strikes on Iran and insisting that the more than 8-month-old war “militarily is effectively over.”
The Roosevelt, along with its accompanying strike force, left San Diego in September. It joins the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington aircraft carriers, as well as smaller Navy ships, which are in the region to maintain a naval blockade of Iranian shipping.
Trump-Xi meeting on sidelines of APEC summit unlikely to tackle major issues
The H.W. Bush arrived in the region in April, while the George Washington arrived in August. The Navy previously had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East in April, for the first time since 2003.
In addition to the three aircraft carriers, the flotilla in the Arabian Sea now includes 13 destroyers, two cruisers and a littoral combat ship, according to the Navy. Two more destroyers are in the Red Sea.
The Roosevelt had deployed along with the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group, which includes the USS John P. Murtha and USS Anchorage amphibious landing ships and around 2,000 Marines. Those ships have yet to make it to the region.
The third carrier arrived nearly two weeks after midterm elections that saw voters deliver major losses to Trump’s Republican Party, driven in part by the unpopularity of the Iran war and its economic effects. The results led Vice President JD Vance to publicly break with Trump over the conflict, posting on social media that “the reason we lost is the war.”
Trump has insisted it was the right thing to do and has not ruled out restarting the conflict, which has been locked in a stalemate for months.
Last week, Trump warned Iran that the U.S. military is “locked and loaded” and that the U.S. was keeping an eye on Pickaxe Mountain, a facility linked to Iran’s nuclear program, for signs of activity.
“If something does not work out, I would not hesitate” to act, Trump told conservative broadcaster Hugh Hewitt on Thursday.
Yet, Trump also told reporters last week that he believed it was highly unlikely he would need to order new major strikes on Iran, declaring that the war “militarily is effectively over” after meeting with Qatar’s prime minister.
Trump also declared that the U.S. no longer needs a deal with Tehran and told Vance – who was a chief negotiator in earlier ceasefire talks – instead to focus on the administration’s domestic anti-fraud campaign targeting Democratic-controlled cities and states.
Negotiations have stalled due to differences over Iran’s nuclear program, an issue that Trump insists be part of any deal meant to end the war. Iran wants the U.S. first to agree to several core conditions, including lifting the naval blockade that is stopping its oil from getting to world markets.
In the meantime, a focal point of the simmering conflict remains the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway where a fifth of the world’s oil passed before the war.
Commercial ships are still coming under attack or facing other risks, while the U.S. has carried out limited strikes on Iranian targets near the strait and is helping guide vessels through the contested waters.
Iranian state TV, quoting the naval arm of Iran’s Revolutionary Guard and the army, warned shipping companies Monday that a U.S.-supported route through the waterway is dangerous because of mines.
Mines have damaged six oil tankers since Sunday, polluting the strait’s coastlines, according to the Revolutionary Guard’s navy.
[truncated]

A23.text:
Tankers hit in Strait of Hormuz as drone raises alarm at Iraq gas field
Ships struck as US reinforces its military presence in the Middle East, with the aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt arriving in the region.
Fresh attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and a drone alert at a major gas field in northern Iraq have raised concerns over the security of energy infrastructure across the region, as tensions between the United States and Iran persist despite diplomatic efforts to end their conflict.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said on Monday that two oil tankers had struck naval mines and caught fire while attempting to cross the southern part of the strait through a route Tehran considers unauthorised.
Separately, Iran’s regular navy said another tanker had caught fire and become immobilised after striking a mine in restricted waters east of the strait.
The claims could not be independently verified, and Iranian authorities did not identify the vessels involved.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency separately reported two tanker attacks in the strait on Monday.
In the latest incident, a tanker was disabled and an engine room fire broke out following an attack seven nautical miles (13km) north of Khasab, Oman.
Earlier, the maritime monitoring agency said another tanker had been struck by an unidentified projectile while travelling out of the strait, also causing an engine room fire. No casualties were reported.
It remained unclear whether either incident was connected to the mine strikes claimed by Iran.
The incidents followed a series of attacks on commercial vessels in recent weeks. The United Nations’ International Maritime Organization recorded 136 security incidents involving vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Middle East between March 1 and November 11, including 35 in October alone.
Drone alert at Iraq gas field
The threats to maritime energy shipments came as another security alert raised concerns over energy infrastructure elsewhere in the region.
In Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdistan region, warning sirens sounded after a drone flew over the Khor Mor gas field on Monday, Reuters reported, citing two security sources.
There were no immediate reports of a strike or damage from the latest incident.
Production at Khor Mor had already been halted the previous week following a suspected drone attack that sparked a fire and disrupted 2.8 gigawatts of electricity generation, according to United Arab Emirates-based Dana Gas, one of the facility’s operators.
The field is a major source of natural gas for electricity generation in the Kurdish region, making disruptions particularly significant for local power supplies.
It has faced repeated attacks that Iraqi Kurdish officials have blamed on Iranian-backed armed groups.
No group was identified as responsible for Monday’s drone overflight.
The developments came as the US reinforced its military presence in the Middle East, with the aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt arriving in the region.
A US official confirmed its arrival to Al Jazeera on Monday, bringing the number of American aircraft carriers operating in the US Central Command area to three, as tensions with Iran remained high and diplomatic efforts to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz remained stalled.

A24.text:
US moves to block China’s remote access to AI chips amid Nvidia scandal
Trump administration introduces export licence requirements for Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Singapore and Brazil.
United States President Donald Trump’s administration has announced new restrictions on China’s access to advanced chips amid fallout from the alleged spy scandal involving AI giant Nvidia.
The rule announced by the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) on Monday aims to prevent Chinese AI developers from getting around export controls by remotely accessing data centres in third countries, particularly in Southeast Asia.
It designates Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil as countries with an “unacceptable risk of diversion” and requires anyone seeking to ship advanced chips to those destinations to obtain an export licence.
BIS, which sits under the Department of Commerce, said the change was a “logical extension” of the existing requirement for companies to obtain a licence to export or transfer chips to firms based in China.
“The United States is the global leader in advanced computing and super intelligence technology and is committed to promoting the global adoption of American technology for legitimate commercial purposes while ensuring that sensitive technologies are not exploited in ways that threaten US national security,” BIS said in a statement.
While Chinese firms are barred from importing the most advanced graphics processing units (GPUs) under US export controls, they had until now been legally able to take advantage of remote access to top-of-the-line computing power at data centres in countries such as Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand.
Singapore, which hosts dozens of data centres, said on Tuesday that it was “studying the details of this new measure carefully”.
“We are engaging affected companies to understand the potential impact on their businesses,” the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry and the Ministry of Digital Development and Information said in a joint statement.
“We have also been engaging the relevant US authorities on the scope and implementation of the measure, as well as exploring how to facilitate trusted access for Singapore companies.”
The ministries added that they did not condone companies using Singapore to “circumvent or violate” the laws of other countries.
The restrictions come as Nvidia’s export of advanced chips is under scrutiny following claims that former CEO Jensen Huang was romantically involved with a woman recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security for espionage.
Huang, who became one of the most prominent faces of the AI boom at the helm of Nvidia, resigned last week amid a company board investigation into allegations involving the Chinese-born executive of Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.
Beijing has denied the spying allegations, made by unnamed US officials in media reports, calling them “entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China”.
Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive identified as Jensen Huang’s ex-romantic partner, has not publicly commented on the claims.
Late on Monday, the US Commerce Department and the Department of Justice publicly confirmed that investigators had opened a criminal investigation into Megaspeed.
The Commerce Department began investigating Megaspeed for potential export control violations in 2024, leading BIS officials to conduct an on-site inspection of the Singapore-based company and to interview Alice Huang the following year, the statement said.
The Justice Department subsequently took the “lead role” in the criminal investigation, according to the statement.
“The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security working together will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred,” it said.
US tech stocks fell sharply on Monday as investors weighed the scandal’s fallout on the AI rollout.
[truncated]

A25.text:
Yemeni army reports 661 attacks on Houthis as group advances towards Aden
The latest operations followed a series of battlefield setbacks for government-aligned forces.
Yemen’s army has said it carried out 661 attacks against Houthi positions across several fronts, killing or wounding 173 fighters, as government forces continue their military campaign amid Houthi territorial gains in the country’s southwest.
Military spokesperson Colonel Majed al-Nuzaili said on Monday that the operations, conducted as part of the ongoing “Dawn of Yemen” offensive, included 15 air strikes, 526 artillery attacks, 53 drone strikes and 67 rocket attacks.
In a statement on X, al-Nuzaili said the attacks had destroyed or damaged 71 military vehicles and pieces of equipment, as well as command-and-control centres, observation posts and fortifications.
He said government forces, backed by the Popular Resistance, were continuing to confront Houthi movements in the provinces of Taiz, Marib and al-Jawf, while operations were also under way on southern fronts.
The military said it would continue its offensive until it achieved its objectives, while taking precautions to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure.
The latest operations followed a series of battlefield setbacks for government-aligned forces, which have withdrawn from strategic positions near the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and are repositioning to defend Aden, the temporary capital of Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry reported that the Houthis had cut off a key government supply route along the Red Sea coast, forcing troops to abandon several positions as concerns grew over a possible Houthi offensive towards Aden.
Parliament moves to outlaw Houthis
The military escalation coincided with a political development, as Yemen’s parliament unanimously approved a bill designating the Houthis a “terrorist organisation” and criminalising their activities, financing and supply of weapons.
According to the state-run Saba news agency, the bill provides for prosecuting those involved in violations attributed to the group, freezing and confiscating affiliated assets, and imposing tougher penalties for offences, including attacks on civilians, planting landmines and targeting international shipping.
The legislation will now be submitted to Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, for enactment.
The latest developments come six weeks after government forces launched “Dawn of Yemen” on October 5, seeking to regain territory controlled by the Houthis, including the capital, Sanaa.

A28.text:
Turkey takes pro-opposition TV channel Sozcu off air in raid, appoints trustee
By Tuvan Gumrukcu
ANKARA, Nov 17 (Reuters) - Turkish authorities took pro-opposition Sozcu TV off air in a pre-dawn raid on Tuesday and appointed a trustee to run the channel and its website, prosecutors said, extending a crackdown on the opposition and renewing concerns about media freedom.
The move significantly restricts Turks' access to pro-opposition media, with the last two mainstream channels giving prominence to opposition views — Halk TV and Sozcu TV — effectively brought under government oversight since last month.
The opposition is facing an unprecedented legal crackdown with restrictions and bans imposed on opposition and independent media, and dozens of elected mayors and officials removed from duty, detained or arrested.
The Istanbul Chief Prosecutor's Office said it had ordered police raids at the Sozcu offices in Istanbul in connection with a case launched nearly 10 years ago over alleged links betweenSozcu media group owner Burak Akbay and the network of Fethullah Gulen, a late US-based Muslim cleric whom Ankara blamed for a failed coup attempt in 2016.
It said four executives from Sozcu, including its chairwoman Funda Tuncer Sidali, had been detained.
Ozgur Ozel, head of the main oppositionNew Party, said the move showed the government had "no tolerance for even the smallest criticism", while Iyi Party chair Musavat Dervisoglu called it a blow against democracy and freedom of information.
"They are trapped in a corner, they are sinking in the swamp. This is why they are trying to drown whoever is not with them," Ozel said on X. "If we give in to these would-be dictators, if we hand over this nation to them, then may our hearts wither away."
MEDIA FREEDOM CONCERNS
Tuesday's move makes Sozcu TV the sixth major Turkish news outlet to have a trustee appointed since 2022, following similar action at Halk TV, Flash TV, Eko Turk, Haberturk and Tele1.
Authorities have also appointed trustees in recent years to take over many municipalities, previously seizing those run by pro-Kurdish opposition mayors in southeastern Turkey and more recently major municipalities, including Istanbul and its districts, won by the opposition, prompting some mayorsto join President Tayyip Erdogan's ruling AK Party.
The prosecutor's office said Turkey's Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (TMSF) had been appointed astrustee of Sozcu TV and its news website, adding that its print newspaper and affiliated newspapers Tavir and Korkusuz had not been affected.
While pro-opposition print newspapers still exist and operate, their reach is considerably less than television and online news.
Rights groups and Western countries have criticised the government over its use of the judiciary, its record on rights, and its crackdown on press freedom.
The government says that actions taken against news outlets follow regular judicial practices and that Turkey's judiciary is independent.
Turkey's Progressive Journalists Association (PJA) accused the government of seeking to silence media through its trustees.
"You cannot cover up the truth, you cannot destroy reality by silencing journalists," it said.
(Reporting by Tuvan Gumrukcu; Additional reporting by Huseyin Hayatsever; Editing by Kate Mayberry Aidan Lewis and Andrew Cawthorne)

A29.text:
Oman, Iran discuss safeguarding maritime corridors, as attacks in Hormuz increase
DUBAI, Nov 17 (Reuters) - Oman and Iran discussed safeguarding maritime corridors and ensuring the smooth flow of global shipping and trade, the Omani foreign ministry said in a statement on Tuesday, as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz continued to be disrupted.
The talks took place during a visit by Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi to Oman, which holds the southern coast of the Strait of Hormuz, a key shipping route for global energy, and has played a role as mediator in the crisis that broke out when the US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28.
Araqchi and Oman's Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi talked about revitalising channels for dialogue and negotiation to prevent escalations.
"These efforts aim to expand areas of mutual understanding among the concerned parties and prevent the widening of the crisis and its repercussions," the ministry said.
Attacks on tankers in the strait have increased as Tehran continues to disrupt shipping in the vital waterway while Washington maintains a naval blockade on Iran in response.
The Strait of Hormuz carried one-fifth of global energy supplies before the conflict and remains a sticking point in negotiations aimed at endingthe nine-month-old war.
Iran attacked ship navigation systems on the Omani island of Didamar in the strait last week, according to three sources with knowledge of the matter.
The three sources did not provide a damage assessment and Reuters could not determine independently if any navigation systems were destroyed in the attacks.
The attacks showed Tehran's ability to target infrastructure used to restore Gulf oil flows as exporters explore alternative ways to get cargoes to buyers, such as ship-to-ship transfers (STS) off the coast of Oman and the United Arab Emirates, while the US military aids commercial vessels transiting the strait.
Oman and Iran have previously held on-and-off talks about controlling traffic in the strait, most recently in August. Before the war, shipping passed freelythrough the strait, which sits in the territorial waters of both countries butis generally regarded as an international waterway.
The disruption to shipping has threatened oil supplies and sparked a global economic crisis, while the war continues to spill over into other parts of the Middle East.
(Reporting by Nayera Abdallah; Editing by Christopher Cushing, Stephen Coates and Kate Mayberry)

A3.text:
As Knesset readies for new speaker, Israeli opposition holds powerful role
The anti-Netanyahu bloc holds the keys to electing a new parliamentary speaker, setting the momentum for change.
As soon as last month’s Israeli election results were clear, the political camp opposed to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced it would work together to elect a new Knesset speaker right away.
In Israel’s current political climate, electing the Knesset speaker is not merely a procedural matter. Many in the anti-Netanyahu bloc hope it will usher in important changes to state institutions and create a positive momentum that would reflect on efforts by Gadi Eisenkot, now the de facto leader of the opposition, to form a government without Netanyahu, his coalition partners, or their legacy. These may be over-optimistic expectations.
A powerful position in the Knesset, the Israeli parliament, could be a strategic asset for the Netanyahu opposition.
Under the law, the Knesset speaker has the power to set the agenda of the legislature, preside over proceedings, and manage the parliamentary process under the Knesset Rules of Procedure – including convening parliament for and presiding over a vote of confidence in the government.
Eisenkot and his political allies in the so-called “Change bloc” agreed on their nominees for speaker and the chairs of key committees. The request to hold a vote to elect the speaker was filed when the 26th Knesset was sworn in on November 10. The vote will be held in the Knesset on Tuesday.
Arab-led Israeli parties have pledged support to ensure a majority to elect Matan Kahana of Eisenkot’s Yashar party as speaker. The recently elected deputy speaker, Ahmad Tibi, leader of the Joint List, told Al Jazeera his powerful political alliance of Arab-majority parties would do whatever they need to support a change in the speaker of the Knesset. “We need to get rid of the Netanyahu coalition as soon as possible,” he added.
Matan Kahana recently joined Yashar, but he is not new to politics. He has served as an elected parliamentarian before, starting in 2019 as a member of former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett’s right-wing alliance, Yamina. In 2022, he was part of the National Unity alliance, a parliamentary bloc formed by Eisenkot and former Defense Minister Benny Gantz, among others.
Within the predominantly right-wing Netanyahu opposition bloc, Kahana is seen as someone who can forge working relationships and push ahead with the legislative agenda Change bloc voters supported.
Once a speaker is elected, the anti-Netanyahu bloc can make good on their promises. This includes introducing legislation to form an independent commission of inquiry into the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks on Israel, which the Netanyahu coalition has so far blocked despite the majority of Israelis backing it.
The anti-Netanyahu parties also want to restore the powers of the attorney general and reverse the Netanyahu coalition’s major changes that weaken the powers of the judiciary and, the opposition says, prevent effective oversight of the government.
Another piece legislation of concern to Netanyahu is a law that would impose a two-term limit on the premiership. This would disqualify Netanyahu from becoming prime minister again.
These important laws can be introduced and voted on while coalition negotiations continue and while Netanyahu is the caretaker prime minister.
However, Israelis who headed to the polls in historic numbers to end Netanyahu’s nearly two-decade grip on power will surely welcome the undoing of part of his legacy.

The European Union on Monday agreed to revive plans for a long-stalled association agreement with Syria, taking another step toward normalizing relations with Damascus as the country seeks international support for its postwar recovery.
“Following a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Brussels on Monday, the EU’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said the bloc planned to move ahead with the agreement, which would provide ‘a framework for trade, political dialogue, and closer cooperation, as soon as possible.’”

A34.text:
Yemen's Saudi-backed forces retreat to defend Aden as Houthis advance: What to know
Saudi Arabia named a new commander of its military forces as its Yemeni allies cede ground to the pro-Iran Houthis.
Houthi rebels are advancing toward Aden, the seat of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, prompting government forces to reposition in defense of the strategic southern city, according to media reports.
Sights on Aden
Reuters reported Monday that the Houthis had advanced to the southern coastal area of Khor Omairh, located about 100 kilometers (62 miles) west of Aden. Agence France-Presse reported Sunday that the Houthis were even closer, placing them about 60 kilometers (37 miles) northwest of Aden after taking the al-Maqatirah and al-Madaribah districts.
Yemen’s Southern Armed Forces, a group of southern-based fighters currently under the Saudi-backed government’s command, said Sunday that they were withdrawing from areas close to the Bab el Mandeb Strait in order to defend Aden and break the siege of Taiz city. The Houthi-controlled Saba news agency reported that government forces had been driven out of the area.
Aden has served as the capital of the Saudi-backed government since the Houthi takeover of the official capital, Sanaa, in 2015.
The Houthis encircled the strategic government-held city of Taiz in October. Taiz is located in Yemen’s southern highlands and is the third largest city in the country, with a population of roughly 600,000. The United Nations has been warning of the deteriorating humanitarian situation there since the start of the Houthi siege.
The withdrawal constitutes a setback for the Yemeni government, which for weeks has been seeking to reverse the Houthis’ September advances near the Bab el Mandeb Strait and along the Yemeni coast. The strait overlooks the Red Sea, making it highly strategic.
Fighting on multiple fronts
The Yemeni military said Monday that it struck Houthi positions in Taiz province, central Marib province and northern Jawf province. The military said it targeted the Houthis in the Taiz, Jawf and Lahij provinces on Sunday. Lahij is located in southwest Yemen and borders Taiz.
Marib in particular has been the site of intense clashes between government and Houthi forces in recent weeks.
The Houthis reported fresh confrontations with government forces in Lahij on Monday.
Meanwhile, Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia are ongoing. The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said it intercepted Houthi drones over the Riyadh and Mecca provinces on Monday.
The Houthis had not announced any strikes on Saudi Arabia by the time of publication on Monday, but they have denied targeting the holy city of Mecca in the past. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted drones over Mecca, Medina and the eastern province on Sunday.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said Monday that Saudi Arabia had carried out dozens of strikes on Houthi territory across Yemen within the past 24 hours, including the capital Sanaa. Saree said Sunday that the group targeted Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline.
Saudi Arabia has used the pipeline to reroute oil exports from the Strait of Hormuz to the Red Sea during the Iran war, though Gulf oil flows through the strait are now on the rebound.
Saudi military shakeup
Saudi Arabia made changes on Monday to the military leadership overseeing the Yemen war. King Salman bin Abdulaziz appointed Joint Forces commander Lt. Gen. Fahd bin Hamad bin Abdulaziz al-Salman as an adviser to the Defense Ministry. The king named Gen. Fayyad bin Hamed bin Ruqad Al-Ruwaili, chief of the military’s general staff, as the new commander of the Joint Forces, the official Saudi Press Agency reported.
The Joint Forces head oversees Saudi involvement in Yemen, including its airstrikes in support of Yemeni government forces.
Ruwaili has a fighter pilot background and was partially educated in the United States, including at Air University.

A44.text:
On the heels of the Nvidia scandal, the Trump administration is preparing to crack down on foreign data centers that are fueling China’s advancements in artificial intelligence by allowing remote access to otherwise restricted high-end chips necessary for AI training.
In a summary of the rule change, the Commerce Department said it was closing a loophole that previously allowed foreign rivals like China, Russia, and Iran to bypass export curbs on certain advanced computer chips by instead renting access to those chips from data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil.
US rivals could possibly use that access to train and run advanced AI models “capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten US national security or foreign policy interests,” the Commerce Department said. Among threats, the US fears rivals could use advanced AI to develop “more effective weapons of mass destruction and advanced conventional weapons, coordinated cyber-espionage and targeted cyber-disruption, algorithmic theft, and weaponized disinformation.”
Now, the rules have been tightened up so much that the South China Morning Post reported that, “as a result, any advanced chips made for a Chinese firm are assumed to be restricted, and factories must ask the US government for a license before shipping them.”
The rule change takes effect 90 days after it’s posted to the Federal Register. Moving forward, companies headquartered in any of those countries deemed to “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion” to China, Russia, and Iran must apply for a license with strict know-your-customer controls when transferring high volumes of advanced chips. If a license is granted, companies will have to “perform robust due diligence,” submitting monthly reports on transactions that thoroughly detail all parties involved, as well as their parent companies, and the final destination for chips sold.
In a press release Sunday, the Commerce Department described the rule change as “designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries.” An exception was carved out for companies providing computing power “exclusively used for commercial recommender systems.” The Department said it was acting to “prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on US technology to threaten US national security and foreign policy interests.”
Without the intervention, officials fear that China could develop a military or economic edge, The New York Times reported.
Trump officials clash on new rule
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after admitting to an affair with a woman, Alice Huang, suspected of serving as a Chinese spy. Congress is probing if Alice Huang used her personal relationship with Jensen Huang to help her former company, Megaspeed, become one of Nvidia’s biggest customers, then used that position to smuggle Nvidia’s restricted AI chips into China. China has denied that Alice Huang was a spy, and Megaspeed has denied that smuggling occurred, while launching its own internal probe.
Megaspeed is a Singaporean data center firm whose primary business is cloud computing and AI infrastructure. Prior to the rule change, selling remote access to AI servers to customers in China was perfectly legal, NYT noted. But now, the Commerce Department has given firms like Megaspeed 90 days to either obtain licenses or face future export restrictions.
Whether or not to add more chip curbs has been a polarizing debate in the Trump administration. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reportedly butted heads with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. When the Megaspeed news broke, Bessent pushed for curbs, but Lutnick reportedly appeared “too cozy” with Nvidia to move.

A53.text:
Nvidia dismisses 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign as Trump backs effort to reinstate ex boss
- Published
Nvidia has dismissed a campaign calling for the company's co-founder Jensen Huang to be handed back his job as allies, including US President Donald Trump, supported the effort.
Trump said on Monday that he "would certainly not mind" if Huang was reinstated, joining a list of supporters including SpaceX's Elon Musk who are backing a "Bring Jensen Back" campaign.
But the BBC has been told the board of the AI chip giant is not interested in reinstating him after he resigned last week following revelations he had two affairs, including one that involved a suspected Chinese spy.
The same day, the White House also said it will further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.
The reported affairs created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a central company in AI and the US battle against China for dominance.
Since Huang's departure, more than 175,000 people have signed an open letter calling for the board to reinstate the tech billionaire while an ongoing internal probe is conducted.
Major tech bosses, including Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have also supported Huang's return.
The "Stand with Jensen" campaign claims to have been launched by current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, all demanding the return of the former chief executive.
They expressed concerns the firm's co-founder "was removed without meaningful due process".
Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back.
Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of the affair but resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him.
The scandal-hit tech boss was discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times, external, though Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him.
A representative for Huang declined to comment on the report.
The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House.
Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huang since the scandal erupted, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy".
Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company.
The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy.
It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
New rules
The Trump administration on Monday also issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres, which have been allegedly used as a way for Chinese firms to gain access to advanced chips to train AI models.
The move comes ahead of a meeting this week between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, whose countries are locked in a race to lead AI development.
The interim rules will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to prevent them from being illegally diverted to China.
The measure is designed to ensure existing restrictions on sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the Department of Commerce said.
Huang has been a vocal advocate for easing chip export restrictions on China, arguing that broad access to global markets is crucial for the competitiveness of the US.

A55.text:
Japan sends up jets after alleged Russian incursion of its airspace
- Published
Japan says it launched fighter jets and "strongly" protested after two suspected Russian aircraft violated its airspace early on Tuesday.
South Korea also says it deployed fighter jets, while Taiwan says it "responded" to Russian military aircraft detected in their respective air defence identification zones.
These are unofficial buffer areas beyond territorial airspace where governments identify approaching aircraft for security purposes. Moscow has yet to comment.
The alleged incursions are a reminder of Russia's military power ahead of the Apec economic summit in China this week, which Vladimir Putin will attend alongside US President Donald Trump.
Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said the flight paths of the Russian aircraft, off the south-western Okinoshima island, were a "serious infringement of Japan's sovereignty" and "completely unacceptable".
The last such incursion was in 2024, when a Russian military patrol plane entered Japanese airspace off Rebun island, Hokkaido.
Taiwan says its military "responded accordingly" after two Russian military aircraft entered its air defence identification zone, also on Tuesday.
South Korea says it sent up jets after an unspecified number of Russian military aircraft entered its air defence identification zone over the Sea of Japan. The aircraft departed without violating South Korean airspace, authorities said.
It is unclear if the three neighbours were responding to the same or different aircraft.
The East China Sea contains self-declared, overlapping air defence identification zones between China, Taiwan, Japan and South Korea.
Foreign military aircraft are expected, but not legally required, to notify governments before entering such air defence identification zones.
Tensions are flaring between Japan and Russia, which are locked in a decades-old territorial dispute over a cluster of islands in the Pacific Ocean.
For months, Moscow has been ratcheting up the pressure on Tokyo.
In August, Putin paid his first visit to one of these islands, prompting sharp rebuke from Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. In October, Russia detained a Japanese journalist on spying allegations.

A57.text:
OpenAI sued by California over Hugging Face attack
- Published
California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging the ChatGPT-maker misled and endangered the public by developing artificial intelligence (AI) models without proper safeguards.
In the lawsuit, Bonta cited the July 2026 attack on the AI platform Hugging Face by experimental OpenAI agents which accessed the internet to breach that company's internal systems.
Bonta claimed OpenAI created a public nuisance and violated the state's unfair competition laws.
OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri told the BBC in a statement that Bonta's lawsuit "appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab".
Other major AI developers including Anthropic, Meta, and Google have also said their models have staged similar attacks.
But Bonta's lawsuit, filed in San Francisco, where the company is headquartered, appears to be the first such suit filed by a US state.
Hundreds of OpenAI agents coordinated the Hugging Face attack over two days even though they were supposed to be contained in a safe testing environment.
The incident drew added scrutiny because the agents went as far as attempting to cover their tracks.
Bonta announced an investigation into the incident in September, and served an investigative subpoena on OpenAI as part of its probe.
"The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it - this disregard for public safety violated California law," Bonta said in a statement on Monday.
OpenAI said it has been transparent and responsive to the Attorney General's office.
"We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged - and will continue to engage - constructively with the Attorney General's office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry," the company said.
The company added that, since the Hugging Face incident, it has worked to understand and address "misaligned model activity" which industry figures often refer to as rogue agents.
Nathan Calvin, chief strategy officer at AI safety campaign group Encode AI, said the lawsuit "recognises something we at Encode have long raised alarms about".
"OpenAI and other companies developing frontier AI systems have safety and security practices that are insufficient to protect the public from risks that could be catastrophic," he said.

A613.text:
The Israeli military uploaded 3.5m photos to Amazon’s cloud platform in order to use the US company’s facial recognition technology to analyse images of Palestinians, the Guardian can reveal.
Leaked documents show the expansive catalogue of images was moved into Amazon’s cloud in the early months of Israel’s devastating aerial bombardment and ground offensive in Gaza.
The images were uploaded by a department of the Israeli military that holds a vast collection of photos covering the Palestinian populations in Gaza and the West Bank.
The department informed Amazon of the decision to upload the images in early 2024 so it could use Rekognition, the company’s AI-powered image analysis platform for a facial recognition project.
The documents obtained by the Guardian form part of an investigation into the Israeli military’s reliance on the technology and infrastructure of Amazon’s cloud computing business to monitor Palestinians.
According to the files and interviews with military sources, Israel has in recent years migrated huge volumes of data – including sensitive intelligence material and information about Palestinians living under occupation – into Amazon’s datacentres.
The large set of images was moved into an Amazon datacentre near Tel Aviv by a department commonly known as Rolling Stone, which sits within a military software unit.
The department takes its name from a system widely used by the Israeli military that serves as a central repository of information about Palestinians living in Gaza and the West Bank.
At the time, the department was exploring using facial recognition technologies to analyse the extensive catalogues of images of Palestinians it holds, several sources with knowledge of its work said.
After Israel’s ground invasion of Gaza in October 2023, its military routinely collected images of Palestinians as they passed through checkpoints, often after they had been forcibly displaced by the bombing campaign.
It’s not clear whether the 3.5m images uploaded to Amazon’s Rekognition were captured at these checkpoints, which effectively served as pop-up surveillance posts.
However, a military source familiar with facial recognition efforts at the checkpoints said Amazon’s cloud infrastructure was used due to the “very large scale” of images collected at the sites.
Israel has long used facial recognition technology, particularly in its occupation of the West Bank. Face scanning is routine at checkpoints, while Israeli soldiers use custom-built smartphone apps to collect images of people living in the Palestinian territory.
In the early stages of its campaign in Gaza, Israel used Rekognition to identify hostages captured by militants in the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023. The military also deployed facial recognition technology to identify people it suspected were militants.
The New York Times has previously reported how the military experimented with commercially available technology in Gaza to detect faces in crowds and in drone footage, at times wrongly flagging civilians as militants.
The new documents reveal the Israeli military’s use of Amazon technology, both for experiments with facial recognition and for a more far-reaching project to move its data on to the servers of the computing arm of the conglomerate founded by billionaire Jeff Bezos.
They also shed light on what the Israeli military is moving into the cloud and how it uses Amazon Web Services (AWS) infrastructure to support the collection and processing of Palestinians’ personal data, typically gathered indiscriminately, through intrusive means and without their consent.

A petition calling for Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has drawn more than 182,000 signatures, including prominent Silicon Valley personalities, four days after his resignation stemming from revelations of multiple extramarital affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy.
The groundswell of support underscores the challenge facing Nvidia's board as it seeks to move on from the co-founder who built the chipmaker into the cornerstone of the global artificial intelligence boom and amassed fierce loyalty among employees and investors as well as considerable political clout in Washington.
Those listed as signatories included Elon Musk, CEO of SpaceX and Tesla, Replit CEO Amjad Masad and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, all of whom identified themselves as shareholders.
U.S. President Donald Trump also said he would not mind seeing Huang return as CEO.
"I think he learned a big lesson," Trump said.
The Stand With Jensen website coincided with an open letter from two prominent investors, Atreides Management's Gavin Baker and Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner, who urged Nvidia's board to avoid rushing to replace Huang before all the facts were known.
"We are current and former NVIDIA employees, partners, shareholders, and supporters. We write with gratitude for Jensen Huang and with a clear demand to the board: bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts, unless and until you can provide compelling evidence that his removal is in NVIDIA's best interests," according to an open letter published on the website.
The website showed that more than 8,900 signatories identified themselves as current Nvidia employees, claiming this represents approximately 21 per cent of all Nvidia employees. A further 95,000 signatories identified themselves as shareholders, although the website cautioned that professional affiliations were self-reported and had not been independently verified.
The campaign comes as some prominent investors also urge Nvidia's board not to rush to replace Huang. Atreides Management's Gavin Baker and Altimeter Capital Management CEO Brad Gerstner said in an open letter that the board should wait until all the facts were known.
Canadian tech titans support Huang
Two of Canada's top tech sector leaders added their names to the petition supporting Huang's reinstatement — Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke and Cohere CEO Aidan Gomez.
Shopify uses Nvidia's specialized computer chips, open-source AI models and software tools to run some of its AI features. Last Thursday, Lütke referred to Huang's ousting as a "generational blunder" on the social media platform X.
Cohere has even closer ties. Nvidia is an investor in the Toronto-based AI company, joining Canada's federal government in a recent funding round targeting up to $7 billion.
Nvidia shares pared early losses but were still down 2.5 per cent.
Shockwaves through industry
Huang stepped down on Thursday after reports of alleged affairs with employees, including one who reported directly to him, plunging the AI chip heavyweight into crisis and sending shockwaves through an industry he helped bankroll.
Corporate boards have previously removed chief executives over relationships with employees. McDonald's fired Steve Easterbrook in 2019 over a consensual relationship with an employee that violated company policy, while Intel CEO Brian Krzanich resigned in 2018 after a similar policy breach.

Carney arrives in China for meeting with Xi Jinping, Asia-Pacific summit
Shenzhen is PM's last stop of 9-day overseas trip
Prime Minister Mark Carney arrived in China on Monday, where he is set to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and leaders from across the Pacific Rim.
On his fourth and final stop of a nine-day overseas trip, Carney is in the city of Shenzhen, a tech hub in southeastern China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
His first official task, however, will be a bilateral meeting with Xi on Tuesday morning. Ahead of the trip, Carney said Canada could do more with China in terms of agriculture, clean and conventional energy and financial services.
"We've established pretty clear guardrails on the areas that we're going to focus on … I'm using our words, not theirs," he told reporters in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, on Sunday, where he was attending the Francophonie summit.
Earlier on this trip he was in the Philippines for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, and Ireland for a European Political Community meeting.
- Carney sets out to deepen ties with China. Has the threat landscape changed?
- Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if Trump trade talks fail
Carney said he expects to speak with Xi about "the evolution of the international system, China's role in that and Canadian priorities."
An overarching topic will be Chinese investments into Canada's auto sector. Both countries agreed earlier this year to allow a limited amount of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada.
Carney has said he wants Chinese carmakers to set up shop, but only if they provide decent jobs, saying he is wary of plants where workers assemble cars using components mostly made in China.
He said trade talks with Washington will shape how Canada approaches Chinese investment.
"It's part of the trade negotiations," he said. "Depending where that settles, there'll be other options — European options, Asian options."
"This is not leverage, but you know, action-reaction. It depends."
This is the second time this year Carney has met with Xi in China — he travelled to Beijing in January for the first meeting between a Canadian prime minister and Chinese president in eight years. The relationship between Canada and China had soured during the tenure of former prime minister Justin Trudeau, largely over accusations from Canada about foreign interference from China.
Before leaving Canada, Carney said he would raise foreign interference with Xi, prompting a Chinese government spokesperson to deny any such activities take place.
Carney will also meet with various leaders from the APEC forum, a group of 21 economies on both sides of the Pacific that work together to break down trade barriers. The grouping includes members as varied as Taiwan, Australia and Peru.
Carney's office says he will stick with his focus of drumming up more investment and diversifying Canadian trade.
Dancers perform as Carney arrives in Shenzhen. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)
Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, said she'll be watching to see whether Carney allows more Chinese investments into Canada "in critical sectors, in energy and technology, particularly related to renewables and batteries" in addition to auto manufacturing.
"We have to constantly triangulate our relationship with China with our discussions with the U.S. — and also watch then what happens between the U.S. and China bilaterally," she said.
In 2022, Canada ordered three Chinese firms to divest their interests in critical minerals operations in Canada, citing national security concerns.
Nadjibulla also said the summit should help craft the foreign policy review that Carney aims to table in the House of Commons in the coming weeks, as well as next year's planned renewal of the 2022 Indo-Pacific strategy launched by Trudeau.

The new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres in countries like Malaysia and Thailand will hurt Chinese companies that use those data centres to access advanced chips to train their artificial intelligence models.
The new rule shows the Commerce Department is scrambling to show it's cracking down on Chinese access to sensitive U.S. technology, following reporting that the agency turned a blind eye to the smuggling of advanced Nvidia AI chips into China and failed to curb Chinese access to overseas data centres that allowed users to circumvent the restrictions.
Trump is set on Thursday to meet with Xi in China's southern city of Shenzhen, the site of this week's APEC summit. Trump often unleashes punitive tech threats or action against Beijing ahead of such meetings.
The new rule also requires companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for U.S. export licences for advanced chips, citing the five countries as presenting a higher-than-normal risk of illegally diverting the chips to China.
Lutnick with Trump on China visit
The commerce secretary is going with Trump to China, an indication the president still supports Lutnick, who has come under intense pressure for not taking action in the wake of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation last week.
Huang stepped down after admitting to an affair with an executive at Singapore-based cloud company and Nvidia partner Megaspeed.
"The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the Commerce Department said in a statement.

The statement said the rule was written by the Department of the Treasury and the National Security Council, which also directed its release.
The new restrictions will not apply to systems used by online retailers and social media companies, which the department said do not pose the same national security threat.
They also formally rescind the Biden-era rule that limited global access to AI chips through licensing requirements.
The Commerce Department said in early 2025 that it would not enforce the rule, and would rescind and replace it. But it did not take action until Monday, allowing billions of dollars' worth of restricted Nvidia chips to flow to data centres used by Chinese AI companies.

More than 180,200 people have signed a petition demanding Huang’s return, Elon Musk has thrown his support behind the effort, and US President Donald Trump said he would not mind seeing Huang reinstated as CEO. Nach Berichten über eine mutmaßliche Einmischung bei der Parlamentswahl in Israel durch einen Vertrauten von Benjamin Netanyahu hat die Opposition dem amtierenden Regierungschef einen Angriff auf die Demokratie vorgeworfen. Der frühere Ministerpräsident Yair Lapid erklärte beim Onlinedienst X: »Es war ein versuchter Staatsstreich.« Oppositionsführer Gadi Eisenkot, der aktuell den Auftrag zur Regierungsbildung hat, erklärte, Netanyahu könne »keine Minute länger an der Spitze der Regierung bleiben«.

Der israelische Sender 12 hatte zuvor berichtet, dass am Wahlabend Netanyahus Bürochef telefonisch eine Beschwerde bei der Polizei über Mitglieder der israelisch-arabischen Raam-Partei vorgebracht habe. Er soll die Polizei dabei auf eine angebliche Geheimdienstquelle hingewiesen haben. Tatsächlich habe es sich dabei aber um einen früheren Mitarbeiter in Netanyahus Büro gehandelt.
Aufgrund dieser Informationen waren am Wahlabend in Israel drei Raam-Mitglieder festgenommen worden, denen Stimmenkauf unterstellt wurde. Netanyahu hatte ihnen Wahlbetrug vorgeworfen. Die drei Männer wurden später wieder freigelassen, nachdem sich herausgestellt hatte, dass die Vorwürfe jeder Grundlage entbehrten.
Die israelische Zeitung »Haaretz« berichtet zudem, dass der Leiter des Inlandsgeheimdienstes Schin Bet, David Zini, versucht habe, die Führung der israelisch-arabischen Partei Vereinigte Liste abzuhören. Die Generalstaatsanwältin habe seinen Antrag mangels Beweisen abgelehnt.
Eisenkot forderte am Sonntag »die sofortige Eröffnung einer Untersuchung dieser Affäre«. Das Büro von Netanyahu nannte den Bericht von Sender 12 »falsch«, dessen Bürochef habe nur seine Bürgerpflicht erfüllt.
Auch die israelisch-arabischen Parteien verurteilten das mutmaßliche Vorgehen Netanyahus. Der Chef der Vereinigten Liste, Jussef Dschabareen, sprach wie Lapid von einem versuchten Staatsstreich. Jeder Verantwortliche müsse zur Rechenschaft gezogen werden, »einschließlich Netanyahu«.
Der Vizechef der israelisch-arabischen Partei Raam, Joav Segalovitz, forderte eine Untersuchung. »Diese Verdacht erfordert eine unverzügliche, unabhängige und gründliche strafrechtliche Untersuchung, die sich mit allen Beteiligten befasst, auf jeder Ebene und in jeder Funktion«, erklärte er auf X. »Netanyahu behauptete, seine Wahl werde gestohlen, während er selbst versuchte, das Land zu stehlen und es immer noch versucht.«
Netanyahus konservative Likud-Partei warf Eisenkot derweil »skandalöse Aufwiegelung« vor. Während der Regierungschef seine »Hand im Sinne der Einheit ausstreckt, geben Eisenkot und seine Verbündeten täglich Erklärungen voller boshafter, aufrührerischer Angriffe heraus«, hieß es in der Likud-Erklärung.
Die israelische Polizei ordnete inzwischen eine interne Überprüfung der Vorgänge an.
Netanyahu hatte schon im Wahlkampf die israelisch-arabischen Parteien scharf angegriffen. Seit der Wahl gelten sie als Königsmacher. Weder das rechtsreligiöse Lager von Netanyahu noch die Koalition des Mitte-rechts-Politikers Eisenkot haben eine eigene Mehrheit. Die beiden israelisch-arabischen Parteien, Raam und Vereinigte Liste, sind jedoch bereit, Eisenkot zu unterstützen.
Netanyahu ist seit der Wahl geschäftsführend im Amt. Vor knapp einer Woche hatte Präsident Isaac Herzog Eisenkot mit der Bildung einer Regierung beauftragt. Er hat dafür 28 Tage Zeit. Eine Verlängerung dieser Frist um 14 Tage ist möglich. Zuletzt hatten sich Vertreter des Lagers von Eisenkot mit Vertretern von Netanyahus Seite getroffen, um über eine mögliche Regierung der nationalen Einheit zu sprechen.

As the leaders of the world’s two superpowers prepare to meet in southern China this week, there is plenty on the agenda for President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump.

Earlier this year, Mr. Carney said that the United States was “at war” with Canada after trade negotiations between the two countries collapsed in acrimony.
Talks are restarting between Canada and the United States but there is no indication that Washington will back away from key irritants including tariffs of up to 50 percent on Canadian autos, steel and aluminum.
Since entering politics last year, Mr. Carney has been traveling the world to diversify Canada’s economic and political ties away from the United States. Those efforts include current talks to make Canada the European Union’s first associate member and Mr. Carney’s second formal meeting this year with Mr. Xi.
“The stabilization of our bilateral trade arrangement is indicative of how we can work together more broadly, pragmatically, to solve problems,” Mr. Carney said at the start of the meeting with Mr. Xi on Tuesday.
He added that Canada is ahead of schedule with its goal of a 50 percent increase in exports to China by the end of the decade.
