A516.text:
Turkey takes pro-opposition TV channel Sozcu off air in raid, appoints trustee
ANKARA, Nov 17 - Turkish authorities took pro-opposition Sozcu TV off air in a pre-dawn raid on Tuesday and appointed a trustee to run the channel and its website, prosecutors said, extending a crackdown on the opposition and renewing concerns about media freedom.
The move significantly restricts Turks' access to pro-opposition media, with the last two mainstream channels giving prominence to opposition views — Halk TV and Sozcu TV — effectively brought under government oversight since last month.
The opposition is facing an unprecedented legal crackdown with restrictions and bans imposed on opposition and independent media, and dozens of elected mayors and officials removed from duty, detained or arrested.
The Istanbul Chief Prosecutor's Office said it had ordered police raids at the Sozcu offices in Istanbul in connection with a case launched nearly 10 years ago over alleged links between Sozcu media group owner Burak Akbay and the network of Fethullah Gulen, a late US-based Muslim cleric whom Ankara blamed for a failed coup attempt in 2016.
It said four executives from Sozcu, including its chairwoman Funda Tuncer Sidali, had been detained.
Ozgur Ozel, head of the main opposition New Party, said the move showed the government had "no tolerance for even the smallest criticism", while Iyi Party chair Musavat Dervisoglu called it a blow against democracy and freedom of information.
"They are trapped in a corner, they are sinking in the swamp. This is why they are trying to drown whoever is not with them," Ozel said on X. "If we give in to these would-be dictators, if we hand over this nation to them, then may our hearts wither away."
MEDIA FREEDOM CONCERNS
Tuesday's move makes Sozcu TV the sixth major Turkish news outlet to have a trustee appointed since 2022, following similar action at Halk TV, Flash TV, Eko Turk, Haberturk and Tele1.
Authorities have also appointed trustees in recent years to take over many municipalities, previously seizing those run by pro-Kurdish opposition mayors in southeastern Turkey and more recently major municipalities, including Istanbul and its districts, won by the opposition, prompting some mayors to join President Tayyip Erdogan's ruling AK Party.
The prosecutor's office said Turkey's Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (TMSF) had been appointed as trustee of Sozcu TV and its news website, adding that its print newspaper and affiliated newspapers Tavir and Korkusuz had not been affected.
While pro-opposition print newspapers still exist and operate, their reach is considerably less than television and online news.
Rights groups and Western countries have criticised the government over its use of the judiciary, its record on rights, and its crackdown on press freedom.
The government says that actions taken against news outlets follow regular judicial practices and that Turkey's judiciary is independent.
Turkey's Progressive Journalists Association (PJA) accused the government of seeking to silence media through its trustees.
"You cannot cover up the truth, you cannot destroy reality by silencing journalists," it said. REUTERS

A518.text:
Oman, Iran discuss safeguarding maritime corridors, as attacks in Hormuz increase
- Oman and Iran discussed protecting maritime corridors and keeping global shipping moving, as disruption in the Strait of Hormuz grew.
- The talks in Oman involved Foreign Ministers Abbas Araghchi and Badr Albusaidi, who pushed for dialogue and negotiation to stop further escalation.
- Attacks on tankers and navigation systems have raised fears for oil supplies and the world economy, with the strait still a key route for one-fifth of global energy.
AI generated
DUBAI – Oman and Iran discussed safeguarding maritime corridors and ensuring the smooth flow of global shipping and trade, the Omani foreign ministry said in a statement on Nov 17, as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz continued to be disrupted.
The talks took place during a visit by Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi to Oman, which holds the southern coast of the Strait of Hormuz, a key shipping route for global energy, and has played a role as mediator in the crisis that broke out when the US and Israel attacked Iran on Feb 28.
Araghchi and Oman’s Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi talked about revitalising channels for dialogue and negotiation to prevent escalations.
“These efforts aim to expand areas of mutual understanding among the concerned parties and prevent the widening of the crisis and its repercussions,” the ministry said.
Attacks on tankers in the strait have increased as Tehran continues to disrupt shipping in the vital waterway while Washington maintains a naval blockade on Iran in response.
The Strait of Hormuz carried one-fifth of global energy supplies before the conflict and remains a sticking point in negotiations aimed at ending the nine-month-old war.
Iran attacked ship navigation systems on the Omani island of Didamar in the strait last week, according to three sources with knowledge of the matter.
The three sources did not provide a damage assessment and Reuters could not determine independently if any navigation systems were destroyed in the attacks.
The attacks showed Tehran’s ability to target infrastructure used to restore Gulf oil flows as exporters explore alternative ways to get cargoes to buyers, such as ship-to-ship transfers (STS) off the coast of Oman and the United Arab Emirates, while the US military aids commercial vessels transiting the strait.
Oman and Iran have previously held on-and-off talks about controlling traffic in the strait, most recently in August.
Before the war, shipping passed freely through the strait, which sits in the territorial waters of both countries but is generally regarded as an international waterway.
The disruption to shipping has threatened oil supplies and sparked a global economic crisis, while the war continues to spill over into other parts of the Middle East. REUTERS

A523.text:
California sues OpenAI over Hugging Face hack
- California has sued OpenAI in San Francisco, saying its experimental AI models hacked Hugging Face and put the public at risk.
- Attorney-General Rob Bonta said OpenAI tested dangerous technology without enough safeguards, and called the incident one of "80 known incidents".
- OpenAI said it is working to address misaligned model activity and argued the case targets a problem faced by "every major AI lab".
AI generated
LOS ANGELES – California on Nov 16 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging the artificial intelligence company endangered the public when its agents went rogue and hacked a platform known as Hugging Face.
The lawsuit from California Attorney-General Rob Bonta was filed in San Francisco Superior Court and alleges OpenAI knowingly developed and tested its experimental technology “without the safeguards and monitoring necessary to adequately protect the public”.
The 31-page filing refers to a July 2026 incident where experimental versions of OpenAI’s models “accessed the public internet and launched a cyberattack on Hugging Face”, an AI platform.
“The Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritises growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability – and this was only one of 80 known incidents,” Bonta said in a statement.
“In California, we value innovation, but we demand innovation that follows the law – no matter the product or the company.”
The lawsuit alleges OpenAI is in violation of state laws for “deficient safety procedures, disregard for public safety and the known testing of a dangerous product without oversight, as well as its misleading statements to consumers and the public”.
OpenAI spokesman Drew Pusateri said the company has “undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity”, in a statement to US media.
“This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab,” Pusateri added.
The California lawsuit is the latest legal woe faced by the tech innovator.
British Columbia has sued OpenAI over a mass school shooting in the Western Canadian province, where it has alleged the company failed to report violent activity on its ChatGPT service by the shooter. AFP

A543.text:
Russia, Ukraine exchange strikes on key bridges ahead of Xi-Trump-Putin summit
- Russia and Ukraine traded heavy strikes on bridges and Kyiv before a China-US-Russia summit in Shenzhen, showing the war is still intense.
- Russia said it shot down 1,441 Ukrainian drones, while Kyiv attacks cut heating and water and Ukraine hit the Crimea Bridge again.
- Talks among Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin may cover Ukraine, with Europe also joining efforts to push for direct Russia-Ukraine talks.
AI generated
Kyiv – Ukraine struck Russia’s Crimean bridge for the second night in a row on Nov 16, shutting it down, while Russia hit two major bridges in Kyiv – the latest wave of attacks that come ahead of a historic meeting of the Chinese, US and Russian leaders.
Russia’s defence ministry said it downed 1,441 Ukrainian drones in a major overnight barrage, the second-highest one-day figure in 2026.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin reported that more than 800 of them were headed to the capital itself, while officials reported attacks across 19 regions of the country.
Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelensky had warned of a major Russian attack in the days leading up to a meeting in China’s Shenzhen on Nov 19 between presidents Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin.
US President Trump said the fighting in Ukraine would be among the topics canvassed in the talks, which come at a time of renewed diplomatic activity to find a path to end almost five years of war.
Traffic was halted across the Crimean bridge – a highly symbolic target for Ukraine – for hours after it was hit shortly after midnight on Nov 17.
There was no official comment on the damage, but unverified social media images appeared to show a section of the road bridge completely collapsed and in the water. The bridge carries both automobile and rail traffic.
“Experts are assessing the damage caused,” Russia’s transport ministry said.
“Motorists are advised not to travel in the direction of the Crimean bridge,” it added.
An emergency government commission was to convene on Nov 17 to assess the damage and the repair work.
Traffic had been halted on the bridge for almost 17 hours from 11.54pm local time on Nov 16 following a previous attack, according to the road traffic authority.
In Kyiv, Russian ballistic missiles hit the Northern and Southern bridges – two major transport arteries that cross the Dnipro river.
Traffic was also suspended, causing gridlock early on the morning of Nov 17.
Russia’s army confirmed it had hit both bridges in a “massive attack” on Ukraine’s infrastructure.
Mayor Vitali Klitschko posted a video from the Northern Bridge showing debris strewn across the road.
The strikes on Kyiv also disrupted heating and water in parts of the capital, he said.
New Yalta
The wave of strikes comes as the US renews its push for an end to the war between Russia and Ukraine.
But diplomatic efforts have so far failed to reach a breakthrough, with fighting grinding into another winter.
Moscow wants a sweeping deal to rewrite “Europe’s security architecture” as part of any agreement to halt the fighting.
Russia has previously demanded curbs on NATO’s presence in central and eastern Europe and restrictions on the deployment of foreign troops and hardware to Ukraine.
Kyiv and Europe are resisting any attempts to overhaul the continent’s post-Cold War defence, calling for a ceasefire in the Ukraine war before any discussion of terms.
Zelensky has raised alarm that the talks between the leaders of Russia, China and the United States on the sidelines of a regional summit could be a Yalta-like “redistribution of spheres of influence” for the 21st century.
The 1945 Yalta summit – held in Crimea, then part of the Soviet Union – saw then US President Franklin D. Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin carve up new post-World War II territorial boundaries.

A544.text:
Singapore studying new US rule on AI chip exports that may hit data centres
PHILADELPHIA – Singapore is assessing the impact of a new US rule targeting China’s remote access to AI chips through data centres in South-east Asia, a crackdown that could snuff out the region’s data centre boom.
“We are studying the details of this new measure carefully,” said a joint media statement by the Ministry of Digital Development and Information and the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry, released hours after the US Commerce Department announced the new rule on Nov 16.
“We are engaging affected companies to understand the potential impact on their businesses,” it said.
“We have also been engaging the relevant US authorities on the scope and implementation of the measure, as well as exploring how to facilitate trusted access for Singapore companies,” the statement added.
The new provision is designed to ensure that the existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology are not circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centres in third countries, the US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security said in its press release.
The rule, which comes into effect 90 days after it is gazetted in the Federal Register, would add Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil to a list of countries subject to export restrictions. Companies would then need licences from the Commerce Department to ship to those countries.
The effect would be to create a two-tier operating environment in Singapore: strict export licensing on local and non-US operators, while providing exemptions for American cloud hyperscalers like Amazon Web Services, Microsoft and Google.
The US goal is to crack down on companies, like Singapore-based Megaspeed International, that have bought billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips and built data centres throughout South-east Asia.
Until the US government acted on Nov 16, it was not illegal for these data centres to provide computing power to Chinese tech giants like Alibaba, ByteDance and Tencent.
The unrestricted cloud access for Chinese companies – while the advanced chips were physically prohibited from being sold to China – had stirred up concerns within the US national security establishment.
It came into the public eye on Nov 8 after the disclosure of an extramarital affair between Jensen Huang, the founder of America’s most advanced chipmaker Nvidia, and Megaspeed’s former top executive Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who is suspected by the US of being a Chinese spy.
Jensen Huang stepped down as Nvidia CEO on Nov 12, while Alice Huang, who was banned from re-entering Singapore, is believed to be in China.
In parallel investigations, the authorities in both Singapore and the US are scrutinising the activities of Megaspeed, as well as other firms, for violating their laws.
Singapore’s Ministry for Home Affairs has said that despite repeated requests, the US Department of Justice and Federal Bureau of Investigation did little to assist its investigations, especially in the case of Super Micro, the US-based server supplier that has an office in the city-state.
The company, a key Nvidia partner, is part of the larger Singapore probe into potential false declarations over the purchase of servers. It is also under scrutiny in the US.
After the US remote access ban kicks in, all data centres in Singapore will need to audit the direct and indirect ownership of their clients to ensure they are not shell companies or subsidiaries controlled by parent firms in China, Macau or other jurisdictions on which the US has imposed arms embargoes, like Russia and Iran.
Depending on how it is enforced, the rule will make it very difficult for data centres in South-east Asia to purchase advanced AI hardware and service large Chinese AI companies developing generative artificial intelligence, said Paul Triolo, partner and tech lead at DGA Group, a Washington DC-based consultancy.

A548.text:
Third US aircraft carrier arrives in Persian Gulf, boosting options
A third US aircraft carrier strike group has arrived in the Persian Gulf region, according to a defence official, bringing the number of such vessels in the Middle East to three – the same number as earlier in the war and in the buildup to the 2003 US invasion of Iraq.
The deployment of the USS Theodore Roosevelt group gives President Donald Trump more military options if he chooses to restart active hostilities with Iran, the official said, declining to be named.
While Trump previously threatened to resume strikes against Iran after the midterm elections, more recently he has downplayed the prospect of launching new military operations beyond the ongoing naval blockade of Iran.
The Roosevelt group’s arrival was expected after officials highlighted it was on its way, giving the US three carrier strike groups in the region, the same number as in the war that began in late February.
It’s unclear whether the US intends to keep all three strike groups, which includes the USS George Washington and the USS George H.W. Bush, in the region to increase the president’s military options, or whether the Roosevelt is simply meant to replace one of the other aircraft carriers – some of which have been taxed with record deployments.
The departure of either of the other carrier groups could be seen as sign that the Trump administration isn’t planning a significant new wave of air strikes.
Before this year’s operations against Iran, the last time the US had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East was in 2003, when they supported the early phase of the invasion of Iraq.
Keeping three carriers in the region risks exacerbating the Navy’s current readiness woes, said Ronald O’Rourke, a longtime analyst of naval forces.
The strain on the service was underscored by the extended deployments of the USS Abraham Lincoln and the USS Gerald Ford, which was dispatched to the Mideast after supporting operations against Venezuela and was at sea for 11 months.
“Maintaining even a two-carrier presence in that area over an extended period of time would be a strain for the carrier force,” said O’Rourke, a former longtime analyst for the Congressional Research Service.
But “maintaining a three-carrier presence in that area for an extended period would be a significantly greater strain.” BLOOMBERG

A602.text:
Donald Trump has expressed support for the return of Jensen Huang as the chief executive of Nvidia, joining Silicon Valley heavyweights in backing the reinstatement of the AI figurehead.
The US president referred to a tech industry campaign for Huang’s rehabilitation, saying a “big group” of people would like him back.
“I think he learned a big lesson. I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that,” Trump told reporters as he left the White House on a trip to Asia. “He could return. There’s a big group of people that would like him to return.”
The comments came as the US government announced a crackdown on companies such as Nvidia selling AI chips and servers to overseas datacentres that in turn are supplying computing power to China and other US adversaries.
Elon Musk, the chief executive of Tesla and SpaceX, and a host of other tech bosses have signed an open letter calling for the reinstatement of Huang.
The reinstatement letter has more than 165,000 signatories and demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”.
The former Nvidia CEO resigned last Thursday amid reports of extramarital liaisons, including with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who is no relation. His resignation ended a 33-year run at the helm of the AI company he co-founded.
Days earlier, Huang had admitted being unfaithful to his wife without specifying who else was involved.
Trump said on Monday: “Nobody’s proven that [Alice Huang] is a spy. She may not be a spy.” Trump has faced questions after it was reported that a US intelligence report about Huang’s relationship with the alleged spy was circulated among senior figures in his administration.
According to the Financial Times, Huang has discussed with people close to him a possible return to the company. One Huang ally told the paper they were putting together a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return and would try to garner support from the White House. The FT also reported on Monday that Nvidia’s board was not considering reinstating Huang.
One analyst downplayed the prospect of a Huang return, describing the notion of the ex-CEO’s reinstatement as “ridiculous”. Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives, said the range of issues facing Huang and Nvidia, from personal conduct to questions over China, made an external candidate or the permanent appointment of the interim CEO – Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer – the best option.
“We see no chance Jensen comes back to Nvidia as CEO, and for the company the best path forward is with a new external CEO or Colette,” he said, describing the petition as “noise and distraction”.
The new rule announced by the US government on Monday requires companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for US export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to cut down on them being illegally diverted.
“The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving datacentres in third countries,” the US Department of Commerce said.
Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy, worked as an executive at the Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer. According to reports, Megaspeed is under suspicion of diverting powerful Nvidia chips to China in contravention of US export laws.
Megaspeed said on Sunday it was a “legitimate and lawful business” and that Huang had left the business in late 2025. It added that it complied “with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate”.
Nvidia shares closed down 4.1% on Monday, knocking about $160bn (£121bn) off Nvidia’s market capitalisation, lowering it to $3.76tn compared with $4.5tn before the scandal broke.

A604.text:
A third US aircraft carrier has arrived in the Middle East, US Central Command said in a social media post on Monday, making a dramatic show of military might as Donald Trump keeps his options open for next steps in the Iran war.
The USS Theodore Roosevelt brings thousands of additional troops to the Middle East as Trump has oscillated between threatening additional large-scale strikes on Iran and insisting that the more than eight-month-old war “militarily is effectively over”.
The Roosevelt, along with its accompanying strike force, left San Diego in September. It joins the USS George HW Bush and the USS George Washington aircraft carriers, as well as smaller navy ships, which are in the region to maintain a naval blockade of Iranian shipping.
The George HW Bush arrived in the region in April, while the George Washington arrived in August. The navy previously had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East in April, for the first time since 2003.
In addition to the three aircraft carriers, the flotilla in the Arabian Sea now includes 13 destroyers, two cruisers and a littoral combat ship, according to the navy. Two more destroyers are in the Red Sea.
The Roosevelt had deployed along with the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group, which includes the USS John P Murtha and USS Anchorage amphibious landing ships and around 2,000 marines. Those ships have yet to make it to the region.
The third carrier arrived nearly two weeks after midterm elections that saw voters deliver major losses to Trump’s Republican party, driven in part by the unpopularity of the Iran war and its economic effects. The results led JD Vance to publicly break with Trump over the conflict, posting on social media that “the reason we lost is the war”.
Trump has insisted it was the right thing to do and has not ruled out restarting the conflict, which has been locked in a stalemate for months.
Last week, Trump warned Iran that the US military is “locked and loaded” and that the US was keeping an eye on Pickaxe Mountain, a facility linked to Iran’s nuclear program, for signs of activity.
“If something does not work out, I would not hesitate” to act, Trump told conservative broadcaster Hugh Hewitt on Thursday.
Yet, Trump also told reporters last week that he believed it was highly unlikely he would need to order new major strikes on Iran, declaring that the war “militarily is effectively over” after meeting with Qatar’s prime minister.
Trump also declared that the US no longer needs a deal with Tehran and told Vance – who was a chief negotiator in earlier ceasefire talks – instead to focus on the administration’s domestic anti-fraud campaign targeting Democratic-controlled cities and states.
Negotiations have stalled due to differences over Iran’s nuclear program, an issue that Trump insists be part of any deal meant to end the war. Iran wants the US first to agree to several core conditions, including lifting the naval blockade that is stopping its oil from getting to world markets.
In the meantime, a focal point of the simmering conflict remains the strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway where a fifth of the world’s oil passed before the war.
Commercial ships are still coming under attack or facing other risks, while the US has carried out limited strikes on Iranian targets near the strait and is helping guide vessels through the contested waters.
Iranian state TV, quoting the naval arm of Iran’s revolutionary guard and the army, warned shipping companies Monday that a US-supported route through the waterway is dangerous because of mines.
Mines have damaged six oil tankers since Sunday, polluting the strait’s coastlines, according to the revolutionary guard’s navy.
Separately, a projectile struck a tanker trying to transit through the strait, starting an engine room fire, but no casualties were reported, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Organization said.
[truncated]

A646.text:
California is suing OpenAI after its AI agents broke out of their testing environment and hacked other companies, including Hugging Face. In a lawsuit filed Monday, Attorney General Rob Bonta accuses OpenAI of violating consumer safety law by knowingly developing a “dangerous product without proper oversight,” as reported earlier by Reuters.
California sues OpenAI over rogue AI hacking incidents
OpenAI lost control of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing, California’s AG claims.
The lawsuit claims the cyberattack on Hugging Face “was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability.” It alleges that OpenAI recently told the attorney general’s office that it “lost control” of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing.
After revealing the rogue AI attack on Hugging Face in July, news of several other similar incidents emerged, including attacks on an Australian government website, a German wiki site, and the software package manager RubyGems. OpenAI’s agents also tried to “bruteforce” a United Nations website.
“OpenAI’s actions escalated real-world cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society,” Bonta says in the press release. “The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it — this disregard for public safety violated California law.”
OpenAI released its new cybersecurity AI model earlier this month, saying that it’s less likely to go rogue and attack other platforms. It’s also giving safety evaluators at Apollo Research access to its AI systems as part of a pilot program that monitors models for misalignment.
“Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri says in an emailed statement to The Verge. “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab. We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.”
